items.body:
BOOKS
特集『ジョン・コルトレーン生誕100年』
NO. 341
#150 ジェローム・シュミット『ジョン・コルトレーンへの祈り〜日本を聴く』
2026年9月19日
ゲスト・ コントリビューター

text by Philippe Séclier  フィリップ・セクリエ

著者：ジェローム・シュミット
書名：ジョン・コルトレーンへの祈り
版元：ノワール・シュール・ブラン社「タビリア・コレクション」
初版：2026年8月26日
頁数：128ページ
価格：17.50ユーロ。

1966年7月、ジョン・コルトレーンは最初で最後の日本ツアーを行った。それから60年後、彼の生誕100周年を記念して、ジェローム・シュミットは、今なお鮮烈な存在感を放つ音楽を求めて日本列島を旅する。『ジョン・コルトレーンへの祈り』は、北海道から九州まで、今もなお人生の大切な一部を彼に捧げ続ける人々との出会いへと私たちを誘う。

この旅の中心にあるのは、「ジャズ喫茶」と呼ばれるカフェだ。人々がレコードを聴きに集まる場所で、多くの場合、静寂の中で音楽が流れる。何十年にもわたり、オーナーたちはジャズの歴史だけでなく、彼ら自身の人生の物語をも物語るコレクションを築き上げてきた。こうした場所では、音楽との出会いが運命を左右することもあるのだ。

「大阪の迷宮の中の着物」という章は、このことを特に鮮やかに描き出している。6ヶ月にわたる文通と推薦を経て、ジェローム・シュミットは大阪のコルトレーン・ハウスの創設者である藤岡靖洋と出会った。着物を着て自転車を押しながら街を歩くこのコレクターは、最初は訪問者の知識を試そうとした。しかし、やがて控えめな態度は会話へと変わり、二人の散歩は、ほとんど消し去られてしまった風景の中にコルトレーンの存在の痕跡を浮かび上がらせた。

藤岡は1966年のコンサートには参加していなかった。彼の情熱は後に「ジャズ喫茶」で芽生え、『Olé』、そして『OM』との出会いがきっかけとなり、サンスクリット語やインドの精神性を研究するようになった。「自分の音楽を見つけたと確信した」と彼は打ち明ける。この発見から、旅、出会い、書籍、そして写真、サイン、資料の絶え間ない探求が始まった。収集は、作品にアプローチし、理解し、その歴史を伝える手段となった。

しかし、この熱狂は当初の誤解を消し去るものではない。ジェローム・シュミットが集めた証言によれば、日本ツアーの記憶は、単なる即座の成功というよりも、はるかに複雑なものだった。『至上の愛』を聴き慣れたリスナーでさえ、その自由さに戸惑いを覚える。藤岡は、その真意を理解するには時間が必要だと強調する。彼はまた、この自由さを自身の世代の政治的、精神的な願望と結びつける。彼の目には、コルトレーンの音楽は生き方そのものを体現していたのだ。

旅が進むにつれ、熱狂は消えゆくものへの意識と混じり合う。レストランはその用途を変え、目撃者は次第に姿を消し、場所の記憶は、建物のファサードの前で立ち止まる一人の人物の記憶にのみ残る。しかし、物語はこの愛着のエネルギーを保ち続け、藤岡の告白へと至る。「私は、私なりのやり方で、運命を超越した」。

『ジョン・コルトレーンへの祈り』は、音楽が人生を変える力を持っていることを明らかにしている。カフェ、コレクション、そして会話を通して、ジェローム・シュミットは、音楽を聴くことが親密で共有された体験であり続ける日本の姿を描き出す。コルトレーンを称えるため、彼は私たちを、日々彼の音楽と共に生きる人々との出会いへと誘う。（編集部監訳）

フィリップ・セクリエ　Philippe Séclier
1958年、パリ郊外に生まれる。
ジャーナリスト、写真家、シリーズ編集者、展覧会キュレーターとして活動し、長年にわたり写真・建築・旅が交差する領域で作品を制作。その過程で、ピエル・パオロ・パゾリーニ、ロバート・フランク、エド・ルシェといった巨匠たちの足跡をたどる旅も行う。2021年にAtelier EXB（仏語版）およびPrestel（英語版）から出版された建築家・安藤忠雄に関する著書『ATLAS』で高い評価を得る。最新刊に『Keith Jarrett Japan 1976』(arléa)。

Une prière pour John Coltrane : à l’écoute du Japon

En juillet 1966, John Coltrane effectue sa première et unique tournée au Japon. Soixante ans plus tard, à l’heure du centenaire de sa naissance, Jérôme Schmidt parcourt l’archipel sur les traces d’une musique dont la présence demeure vive. Une prière pour John Coltrane nous entraîne d’Hokkaidō à Kyūshū, à la rencontre de ceux qui continuent de lui consacrer une part essentielle de leur existence.

Au cœur de ce voyage, les jazz kissa, ces cafés où l’on vient écouter des disques, souvent en silence. Leurs propriétaires ont rassemblé, au fil des décennies, des collections qui racontent autant l’histoire du jazz que leur propre vie. Dans ces lieux, une découverte musicale peut décider d’un destin.

Le chapitre « Un kimono dans le dédale d’Osaka » en offre une illustration particulièrement vivante. Après six mois de correspondance et de recommandations, Jérôme Schmidt rencontre Yasuhiro Fujioka, l’homme de la Coltrane House d’Osaka. En kimono, poussant son vélo dans les rues de la ville, ce collectionneur commence par éprouver les connaissances de son visiteur. Puis la réserve cède à la conversation, et leur promenade fait resurgir les traces du passage de Coltrane dans un paysage qui les a presque effacées.

Fujioka n’a pas assisté aux concerts de 1966. Sa passion s’est construite ensuite, dans les jazz kissa, avec la découverte d’Olé, puis d’Om, qui le conduira jusqu’à l’étude du sanskrit et des spiritualités indiennes. « Je savais que j’avais trouvé ma musique », confie-t-il. De cette révélation naîtront des voyages, des rencontres, des livres et une recherche incessante de photographies, d’autographes et de documents. Collectionner devient une façon d’approcher l’œuvre, de la comprendre et d’en transmettre l’histoire.

Cette ferveur n’efface pourtant pas les incompréhensions des débuts. Dans les témoignages recueillis par Jérôme Schmidt, le souvenir de la tournée japonaise se révèle plus complexe que celui d’un triomphe immédiat. Des auditeurs encore familiers de A Love Supreme découvrent une musique dont la liberté les désoriente. Fujioka souligne le temps nécessaire pour en mesurer la portée. Il relie aussi cette liberté aux aspirations politiques et spirituelles de sa génération : la musique de Coltrane engage, à ses yeux, une manière de vivre.

Au fil de la marche, l’enthousiasme se mêle à la conscience de ce qui disparaît. Un restaurant a changé de vocation ; les témoins s’éteignent ; la mémoire des lieux ne tient parfois plus qu’à un homme qui s’arrête devant une façade. Mais le récit garde l’énergie de cet attachement, jusqu’à cette confidence de Fujioka : « J’ai dépassé, à mon niveau, mon destin. »

C’est cette capacité d’une musique à transformer une existence que fait entendre Une prière pour John Coltrane. À travers les cafés, les collections et les conversations, Jérôme Schmidt dessine un Japon où l’écoute reste une expérience intime et partagée. Pour célébrer Coltrane, il nous invite à rencontrer ceux qui, jour après jour, continuent de vivre avec sa musique.

Jérôme Schmidt, Une prière pour John Coltrane, éditions Noir sur Blanc, collection Notabilia, 128 pages, 17,50 €.

Philippe Séclier
Né en 1958 en banlieue parisienne.
Journaliste, photographe, directeur de collection et commissaire d’exposition, il travaille depuis de nombreuses années à la croisée de la photographie, de l’architecture et du voyage. Il a ainsi parcouru le monde sur les traces de grands maîtres tels que Pier Paolo Pasolini, Robert Frank et Ed Ruscha. Son livre « ATLAS », consacré à l’architecte Tadao Ando et publié en 2021 par Atelier EXB (édition française) et Prestel (édition anglaise), a été salué par la critique. Son dernier ouvrage, «Keith Jarrett Japan 1976 », est paru aux éditions arléa.

©Roberto Massotti ©Accademia di Santa Cecilia

キース・ジャレットの2016年夏ヨーロッパツアー5都市のうち未発売だったローマ公演のライヴ盤。会場のSala Santa Ceciliaは、ローマ市内の北寄りに位置し、16世紀に始まる長い歴史と、世界最先端の音響を誇るホールで定員は約2,800人、『fennesz+坂本龍一／Live at Sala Santa Cecilia』というライヴ盤もある。この木質感溢れるホールで即興演奏10曲に＜It’s a Lonesome Old Town＞と＜Somewhere Over the Rainbow＞も演奏している。

2016年ソロツアーは、2月9日カーネギーホールに始まり、4月29日ロサンゼルス、5月2日サンフランシスコ、7月3日ブダペスト、6日ボルドー、9日ウィーン、12日ローマ、16日ミュンヘン。このツアーから『Budapest Concert』(ECM2700/01)、『Bordeaux Concert』(ECM2740)、『Munich 2016』(ECM2667/68)、『New Vienna』(ECM2850)がすでにリリースされているので、ヨーロッパツアーから5作目であり最後にリリースされるライヴ録音作品となる。そして、2017年2月15日ニューヨーク・カーネギーホールでのソロコンサートを最後に活動を休止することになる。なおスタンダーズ・トリオは2014年11月30日ニュージャージー・パフォーミング・アーツ・センター(NJPAC)が最後となった。筆者は、2014年11月30日NJPACのスタンダード・トリオと2016年2月9日のカーネギー・ホールでのソロを見届けた。

この時期のキースのソロコンサートでよく見られる構成だが、＜Part I＞は抽象的でパーカッシヴな演奏で、その一見無機的にも思える音列の中に研ぎ澄まされた美しい響きがあり、観客の甘美なメロディへの期待を気持ちよく裏切り先入観を壊しリセットすることで、”沈黙の次に美しい音”へ誘う儀式となっているかも知れない。そこからPartごとに美しいサウンドとフレーズが次々に生み出される。ブルース進行やクラシック的なニュアンスの曲も交えつつ。クライマックスへ。完全即興にこだわりながらも、スタンダードで締めるのも本ツアーでも定番で、その中でも＜Somewhere Over the Rainbow＞と＜It’s a Lonesom Old Town＞は何度も演奏されている。キースのオリジナルを弾いてくれたらという想いも少しありなかなか叶わないけど。ともあれ、＜Somewhere Over the Rainbow＞の絶妙な間合いで紡ぎ出される音列に時間を支配されながら自由になるような感覚に心が溶けていく。＜It’s a Lonesom Old Town＞は、ブルース進行ではないが＜白い夜霧のブルース＞という邦題があり「昭和のムード音楽」に似合う。その妖しさも秘めたメロディを美しく切なくキースの世界に昇華させていく。

他の４公演に比べても、光り輝く音に優しく包まれる様に、すっと心に入ってくる感が際立っていて、それに呼応する温かい拍手、素晴らしいライヴアルバムで一聴をお勧めしたい。現在、キースはニュージャージーで穏やかに暮らしていて、ピアノも弾いている。現在進行形で活きているキースの音楽を想いながら2016年ツアーの貴重な記録の完結版を楽しみたい。

Reiko Nonoyama 野々山玲子 (drums, piano)

1. Improvisation No.9
2. Improvisation No.5
3. Improvisation No.2
4. Improvisation No.16
5. Improvisation No.7
6. Improvisation No.14

Recorded at 2014 studio, Chiryu, Aichi, Japan
May 11th, June 23th, and July 30th, 2026
Recorded, mixed, mastered by Reiko Nonoyama

みずのとう（MizunotoU）はサックスの柳川芳命とドラムスの野々山玲子のデュオユニットである。ふたりが知立のスタジオに3日間籠って吹き込んだ音が、2枚のアルバムとしてリリースされた。ひとつが本盤『陽』であり、もうひとつがデジタル限定の『陰』である。

筆者は、野々山のドラミングについては、横方向に動いてグルーヴを作り出すというよりは、縦方向に積み上げるかたちをつぎつぎに変貌させていくことに独創性があるとみる。それは静的な計画を指向するものではない。野々山が積み上げた構築物の上や横を柳川の音がかすめて飛んでゆき、その関係性に応じて次の構築物に挑むありようが伝わってくる。すなわち構築物じたいも動的な即興の実践によるものだ。

驚いたことに野々山はピアノも弾いているのだが、その動的な姿勢はドラムスと同様である。だが音の貌には愛嬌も相手を騙そうとする底意地の悪さもあって可笑しい。柳川も挑発されて笑っていたのではなかろうか。

もうひとつの大きな驚きは、柳川のサックスの音がかなり透明性を増したように思えることだ。これは音色だけの話ではない。かつて濁りも野蛮も受け容れていたアジアン・ブルースからは外連味が削ぎ落されているようであり、音を出してしまったことへの恥辱など皆無なのではないか。そのうえで野々山と挑むコミュニケーションの音である。

一期一会の即興演奏であることには間違いないが、成熟した大人の対話だということができる。

（文中敬称略）

参考　『みずのとう / 陰』

CONCERTS/LIVE SHOWS
NO. 341
# 1425 「Satoko Fujii Orchestra Tokyo」 Live in Buddy
2026年9月19日
ゲスト・ コントリビューター

text & photo: Michael Pronko マイケル・プロンコ

Satoko Fujii Orchestra Tokyo
July 29, 2026
Live in Buddy 東京・江古田

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Sachi Hayasaka 早坂紗知 – alto sax, soprano sax
Kunihiro Izumi 泉邦宏 – alto sax
Kenichi Matsumoto 松本健一 – tenor sax
Daisuke Fujiwara 藤原大輔 – tenor sax
Ryuichi Yoshida 吉田隆一 – baritone sax
Natsuki Tamura 田村夏樹 – trumpet
Yoshihito Fukumoto 福本佳仁 – trumpet
Takao Watanabe渡 辺隆雄 – trumpet
Yusaku Shirotani 城谷雄策 – trumpet
Yasuyuki Takahashi 高橋保行 – trombone
Toshihiro Koike古 池寿浩 – trombone
Toshiki Nagata 永田利樹 – bass
Akira Horikoshi 堀越彰 – drums

１st.
１　Kitsune（田村夏樹）
２　Karas（藤井郷子）
３　Jizo（田村夏樹）
2nd.
４　Oni（藤井郷子）
５　Noraneko（田村夏樹）
６　Kappa Ondo（田村一二）

藤井郷子オーケストラによる、世界各地を舞台にした壮大なプロジェクトが展開されている。それぞれ異なる拠点を置く５つのバンドとのレコーディングは、ビッグバンド、楽曲、そして集団即興音楽のあり方を探求する上で、極めて興味深い試みと言えるだろう。ニューヨーク、東京、神戸、ベルリン、名古屋という各地のオーケストラが、それぞれどのような違いを持ち、なぜそのような違いが生まれるのか、その点にも関心がそそられる。各オーケストラの新作が相次いでリリースされる中、東京のオーケストラによるライブ録音は、7月29日に「Live in Buddy」で行われた。

形而上学的な問題はさておき、その東京のオーケストラによる演奏は、強烈な熱量を帯び、説得力に満ちた力強いものだった。それぞれの楽曲には日本の文化や神話に登場するキャラクターの名が冠されているが、そうした共通点があるからこそ、かえってそれぞれの楽曲が持つ独自の個性が際立っていた。藤井と、音楽的パートナーである田村夏樹は、大胆さと繊細さを兼ね備えた指揮でオーケストラを率いた。東京を中心とする腕の立つ多彩な顔ぶれのメンバーとライブ録音を行ったことは、見事な選択だったと言えよう。藤井と田村が指揮の役割を分担したことで、楽曲ごとに異なるアプローチや、全く趣の異なる雰囲気が生み出されていた。

まずは田村の指揮による＜Kitsune＞（狐）」から始まった。演奏が始まるとすぐに、オーケストラの持つダイナミックな表現の幅と圧倒的な音の力が解き放たれた。藤井と田村が率いるこのオーケストラは、楽曲の構成と同様に、音の質感を重視したアプローチをとるが、時折り、安定したテンポやジャズ特有のメロディアスなフレージングも顔を覗かせる。ソロ演奏は、あらゆる方向へと奔放に展開していった。＜Karasu＞（烏）」は、速く軽快な曲調で、まるで人の姿をした烏が発する鳴き声のような響きに満ちていた。楽曲の動きは急降下や旋回を繰り返し、美しくも不協和音を響かせるトランペット・ソロやヴォーカル・パフォーマンスがそこにアクセントを加えていく。休息のために速度を落とし、高度を稼ぐように舞い上がり、独自の旋律を紡ぎ出すその曲は、さながら鳥の動きそのもののようであった。

＜Jizo＞（地蔵）（多くの人々に愛される菩薩）は、スケールが大きく大胆で、重低音が響き渡る楽曲だった。そのエネルギーの流れをしっかりと支えていたのは、ドラムの堀越だった。彼はバンドの内で最も柔軟性に富んだメンバーと言えるだろう。新鮮なリズムの躍動感をもって、あらゆる展開に巧みに溶け込んでいた。この曲には、寺院に佇む地蔵の石像のような「重み」がありながらも、音楽へのアプローチにはどこか肩の力が抜けたような余裕が感じられた。「鬼」は、その名の通り恐ろしいほどの力強さを秘めていたが、ある意味では、この夜の演奏の中で最もメロディアスな曲だったといえよう。もっとも、「メロディアス」という言葉は適切ではないかもしれない。それはむしろ、音楽的な質感や特質、そして深みが織りなす「流れ」のようなものだった。このオーケストラは、聴き手の心に強烈な反応を呼び起こすこと、あるいはそうした反応が生まれるきっかけを作ることを目指しているのだ。

＜Noraneko＞＜野良猫＞では、速いテンポと遅いテンポの間を行き来する展開が見られた。堂々とした開放感から一転して秘められた繊細さが顔を出し、彷徨うような感覚と自由な雰囲気が表現されていた。田村はいつものように、全員を自由に解き放ちつつも互いの音を真剣に聴き合う中で何が生まれるかを探るようなスタイルで指揮をとっていた。特にソロの演奏は素晴らしく、ドラムとベースがソリストたちを力強く牽引していた。

おそらく最も感動的だったのは、フィナーレを飾った＜Kappa Ondo＞（河童音頭）だろう。この曲は、日本の特別支援教育の先駆者であった田村の父親によって書かれたものだ。トランペットや様々なシェイカー、ノイズを交えた奔放なイントロで幕を開け、この夜の演奏の中で最も日本的な旋律とリズムが際立つ楽曲だった。ダイナミクスの急激な変化に、日本的な和声の要素やジャズ特有の複雑さが融合し、バンドの溢れんばかりのエネルギーがそれらすべてを包み込んでいた。

まもなくCD『Kappa Ondo』(LIBRA) がリリースされる予定だが、本作はもちろん、このオーケストラの他の録音作品にもぜひ注目いただきたい。どれも聴き応えのある、魅力的な作品ばかりだ。（編集部監訳）

＊このテキストはマイケル・プロンコ氏が運営するブログ「Jazz in Japan」にけいさいされたものです。筆者の同意を得て訳出、転載しました。
原文は；
https://www.jazzinjapan.com/live-reviews-posts/satoko-fujii-orchestra-tokyo

Michael Pronko マイケル・プロンコ
ジャズ・ジャーナリスト。明治学院大学英文学科教授。
カンザス・シティ生まれ。ブラウン大学で哲学を習得。幼少の頃よりジャズに馴染み、ピアノはレッスンを受けるが、ギターを始めその他は独学。世界漫遊を経て20年前に日本に漂着。「ジャパン・タイムズ」「Jazznin」寄稿家。ブログJAZZINJAPAN運営。著者に『A Guide to Jazz in Japan』ほか。

items.body: Photo by Vins Pedata. Courtesy the artist Sven Fritz is an artist from Germany, who has various ongoing projects that explore performance, experimental music, and sound art. We had the chance to converse over email about his latest work, Der Saal tobt, realized under the Ervin Omsk moniker, published by Orange Milk. The interview was edited collaboratively with the artist. David Murrieta Flores (ACL): Hi Sven, could you please talk a bit about the Ervin Omsk project for readers who are unfamiliar with it? Sven Fritz (EO): Hi David, sure. Ervin Omsk is a pseudonym I’ve been using to release experimental electronic music since 2020. The name doesn’t actually have any special meaning; it’s simply an anagram of my two first names. The project began in 2018 with a few musical collages that were strongly connected to the idea of exploring an abstract painting or sculpture in a particular room—in other words, a very spatial approach, in which I combined diverse sounds from a modular system, field recordings, voice, and so on. Fortunately, Orange Milk was willing to release these tracks on tape in 2020, with artwork by Keith Rankin. In 2023, a second album, titled Schmalster Point, was released on vinyl, with artwork by Brenna Murphy. Now the third album, Der Saal tobt, is being released on tape and CD, with artwork by Lukas Schmenger. Ervin Omsk is currently one of several projects I’m working on. However, it’s the only solo project, and therefore also the most intense one. All my other projects are collaborative—for example, most recently with the French musician Amédée de Murcia. Together, we released an album in March on the Italian label Søvn. There’s also the Hui project, which I’m doing together with Johannes Schebler (Baldruin). An album has just been released on Jollies, and another one was released on Nonlocal Research last year. I’m also part of the artist collective Trickster, where I collaborate with other artists to realize scenarios in the sense of a Gesamtkunstwerk. My role here often involves musical performances lasting several hours and spread out over multiple days. All of my projects fall within the realm of experimental electronic music, and Ervin Omsk really benefits from the many experiences I’ve had working with all these other musicians. This applies not only to production, but also to the concerts I play as Ervin Omsk. These performances, however, are more like interpretations or improvised versions of the tracks I release. ACL: As the liner notes describe it, Der Saal tobt is mimicry of an orchestral body. Usually, we would understand such a body as mechanically efficient and well-coordinated, tuned and built through practice. However, the album understands it differently, and the result is slightly opposite: it’s a body that seems “unpracticed”. How do you understand the relationships between these bodies’ organs? How do you understand the differences between the modern, “well-oiled” orchestra and the album’s version of it? EO: I recently went to a concert where a chamber ensemble performed a piece that really moved me. At the same time, I realized that I actually didn’t really know what was going on. I have no academic background in this field. For example, I lack knowledge of music history and theory, notation, instrumentology, the roles within an ensemble, and so on. So I can only form a vague idea of what is happening in this music. I sense its dissonance, complexity, and openness; at times, it almost feels improvised. At the same time, I associate orchestral music with something highbrow and inaccessible. And that would be, so to speak, a different perspective from the outside. I generally have a rather ambivalent relationship with high culture, because it often caters to unchanging expectations and cultivates a kind of institutional sophistication. And in this context, the terms “efficient” and “coordinated” become interesting: these are actually very performance-oriented categories, which I would spontaneously associate with economics and sport. What do they have to do with music? But yes, an orchestra also needs this high degree of functionality, because, for example, it follows an idea or an order in the form of a notation. The musicians ensure that everything runs smoothly because they have mastered their instruments. To put it bluntly, we could argue that a modern, well-oiled orchestra must function—which sounds almost a bit cold and predictable. In music or art, however, I am not interested in categories like “well rehearsed,” “efficient,” and “coordinated” at first. It is rather the state outside these functions that moves me. To me, the intuitive and the seemingly contradictory have always been special qualities. There is, for example, that brief moment when an orchestra or a small ensemble tunes up. It is an undefined jumble of sounds, a wonderful moment of uncertainty. I am fascinated by the orchestra pit and its sound. But I come from a different musical background, both technically and culturally. I only play guitar, I can sing, and I know some things about synths and computer music. So I can’t imitate the orchestra; I can only bring electronic instruments into play, which then, through practice, become their own form of an orchestral body. And the interactions between the organs aren’t without tension; they sometimes get in each other’s way, and they don’t always speak the same language. And that’s what makes their relationships so special to me. There’s no oil here—more like sand in the gears and friction, to stick with your analogy. ACL: What is the process that you follow in order to craft a track? How do you understand the connections between tracks, once they are finished? EO: I can hardly describe it, really. There is no linear or additive process: each track is the result of countless intuitive decisions, right down to the smallest moments. I’m obsessed with details. The computer of course offers infinite possibilities and an overwhelming freedom. But that also means I usually can’t remember how the individual tracks were made. But I’ll try to describe it using the last track on the album as an example—which was actually the first track I produced: Right at the beginning, I made some very simple and short recordings of an alto recorder that I had borrowed from a friend and musician. After sampling and processing these recordings, the flute’s physical qualities were still there—the airiness, the directness, the softness, the hiss, and so on—but I could tune it freely and also control its overtones and noise, among other things. In fact, it suddenly seemed more like a symbol for an entire group of woodwind instruments or like an instrument that wanted to be several at once. And yet it still had something artificial about it. This impression was reinforced by the way it was played. Arpeggiators, whose tempo and rate were modulated by LFOs; animated envelopes that made glissandos possible; and the layering of several abstract flutes at once, varying only in their playing and sound. Then combined and blended with noises and glitches that picked up on the flutes’ patterns and intonations, countered them, and made them seem alien. Then it got a bit crowded, maybe like rush hour at the main train station. So then it was a constant process of sorting, resampling, stretching, compressing, cutting, copying, pasting, deleting, and leaving pauses—until the track was finished. Something like that, very roughly. And as I said, there’s no single process that applies equally to all tracks. Other tracks have undergone several transformations. They were actually finished; then I completely rearranged them in the context of the entire album, because they didn’t feel right within the album’s dynamic, and the sequence of the tracks that unfolds over just 27 minutes. In addition, on this album I deliberately used certain sounds—such as the processed alto recorder— in several tracks, either obviously or just as a trace. And then, for me, all the pieces take place in the same space; they’re close and direct. Photo of Trickster setup by Sven Fritz. Courtesy the artist. ACL: What sort of gear do you use in this process? Thinking of gear less in terms of straightforward tools, and more socially in terms of extensions of your own thoughts and body, what does all this gear allow you to do? What does it inhibit you from doing? EO: I always try not to own too much gear. Even in production, I use only a few very specific and experimental tools so as not to unnecessarily expand the range of possibilities: a small modular system, MIDI controllers, Ableton Live, with digital samplers, sound generators, M4L devices, a few effects, and then a few flutes and microphones. I like the second part of your question. As a child, I played a home organ—two manuals, bass pedals. After that, I played electric guitar and sang for a long time, always in the context of bands. Vocals and guitar, in particular, are two very direct and physical instruments. It’s almost impossible to transfer that feeling to the world of synthesizers and computers, because playing them is less about gestures and more about fine motor skills involving the hands, fingers, eyes and ears: knobs, pads, trackpads, clicking, looking, listening and so on. But when it comes to abstract thinking about music, synthesizers and computers offer another advantage. They expand the scope of what I can imagine musically and put me in a constant state of learning and wonder. It’s sometimes like a rush. Surely also because I don’t understand everything. But in any case, it changes my own perception of sound, because these machines basically function like auditory microscopes. You can dive incredibly deep with your ears and your thoughts. ACL: Going back to the idea of orchestration, do you understand yourself as the orchestra’s director? Perhaps the orchestra itself, as an abstract embodiment? Perhaps the orchestra’s prompt-maker, to use contemporary code? In short – what is your own position within or without the orchestral body of the album? EO: A prompt-maker relies on clear codes or language as commands, right? That wouldn’t be immediate enough. And unfortunately, I don’t know much about the work of a conductor. But if I may set that aside for a moment, it might be something between a conductor and the orchestra itself. Here’s how I picture it: there’s a room full of objects, no musicians. So I rush through the ranks and set these objects into motion, sound, gestures, and relationships with one another. That would be very closely linked to experiences with live performances—both the role of the conductor and the abstract embodiment. Two examples: There’s this collective project called Trickster, which I’ve already mentioned: very irregularly, we realize a series of evenings as an image—no hierarchy, no stage, no beginning, no end, and thus no mood-setting service. In one of the those projects, I arranged 6–8 different speakers, several mixers, an electric guitar, a spontaneous choir of friends, several synthesizers, a percussionist, and two friends playing the French horn and the soprano recorder, spread throughout a room of about 100 square meters. Here, my role was more like that of a conductor who, over the course of about five hours, activated and collaged all of this using clear impulses and several loopers. Charging and discharging the space, playfully and improvisationally. Then recently I put together a live setup for some shows that had to fit into a backpack. A computer, two MIDI controllers, a small semi-modular synthesizer, and a microphone for vocals. Yet I prepared it in such a way that there were always five different instruments that I could play simultaneously. That was a bit demanding, but very direct, all on a small table—more as if I were many instruments, or, if you will, the orchestra itself. Turning knobs, playing pads, plugging in cables, tuning, singing, applying effects, controlling, not controlling. Photo by Matt Favero. Courtesy the artist. ACL: I’d like to return now to the question of mimicry – it’s an aesthetically loaded term, but it’s possible to contrast it with the idea that there is something organic to the body we are listening to in the album. If we understand the album’s body as more of an automaton, what are its possibilities/capacities/abilities when thinking about traditional musical categories of representation like “expression”? EO: Oh, that’s a really tough question, and I’m not sure I fully understand it. Mechanization could also be understood as a rigid and hierarchical process, but the automaton of the album feels alive to me. That would be more like a cyborg, right? But sure, let’s stick with the image of the automaton. I don’t think of it as a concrete thing with a particular physical form, but rather as an abstract machine, as algorithms and processes. In order to see what abilities it has in terms of traditional musical categories, I have to listen to it. So I’ll pretend for a moment that I didn’t build the automaton. At first, it sounds to me like a machine that seems to define its own form, processes, and movements, acrobatic and unpredictable, like a shapeshifter. It leads an inscrutable life of its own. The mistakes it makes are constantly incorporated into its search for form. A complex and delicate act. But only on the first, and perhaps the second, listening. Once you have become familiar with the complexity, the mechanisms, and the glitches, the form and nature of the automaton become clearer. Perhaps that is the moment when we can return to the “category of representation,” once we have understood the language of the automaton. Because “musical expression” may not be as organic, immediate, and human as we like to think. It is also part of a tradition and works through codes, conventions, expectations, and learned gestures—only seemingly self-evident. The automaton, of course, is only indirectly part of this tradition. In this logic, perhaps the ability of the automaton does not lie in “expressing” something in the classical sense, but in using, shifting, exaggerating, or also refusing these codes of expression. It maybe has the potential to transform many different sounds, instruments, gestures, figures, and experiments into a different but nevertheless familiar form of expression. And perhaps through its artificiality and distance it can make something audible that a human body would not do in this way. But the question really is very abstract. I hope I was able to give a somewhat meaningful answer here. Photo by Tobias Ullrich. Courtesy the artist. ACL: You did, thank you! Now, I’m interested in the meaning of the various track titles. There’s a playful overtone about things going wrong, failing in wholesome ways, or simply being the result of an essay in something (the “Memo Grisaille”, for instance, which alludes to the formative, practical painting made in shades of black or grey that emerged in the Renaissance). What links the process through which you made each track with the titles you chose for them? EO: Collecting titles or sentences is an independent process that I and other friends have been practicing since art school. I’m interested in titles because they add an associative layer to the individual track or the entire album. The album artwork by Lukas Schmenger does that too, by the way. Like the artwork, the titles are an important part of the album, even though they only come into the process at a later stage. I think the titles of the album relate in a certain way to its dynamics and moods. So I really associate the album title “Der Saal tobt” with an image of an agitated and unrestrained group of people. A feeling and sound somewhere between threat and excitement maybe. At the same time, it’s important for me to break up some kind of sonic overload with an everyday and blunt remark like “Beim besten Willen,” which rather expresses a refusal or incomprehension. So I also like the laconic quality of titles. With “Memo Grisaille,” though, it wasn’t my intention to trivialize this art-historical term. I simply like the combination of the words in terms of their sound, and the piece has something fragile and searching about it, like a memory that only becomes sharp and distinct in certain moments. So, with each title, there is an association that relates to the mood of the piece—with it or against it. ACL: Your previous album already explored a sense of joy derived from electronic sound interactions. Considering the track title themes, I think the argument can be made that there’s a humorous undercurrent in Der Saal tobt – there’s a philosophical perspective that says, basically, that it’s funny when things act like persons, but also the other way around. As the album’s automaton furiously fumbles around, we could be inspired to laugh: have you ever thought of experimental electronic music as possibly funny? Would you see a role for humor within your work, in the past, now, and in the future? EO: Experimental electronic music can be fun, sure. But so far, I haven’t gotten that feeling from this album. Then again, maybe I’m just missing something because I wasn’t sitting at the instruments or in front of the computer laughing while making it. Maybe it’s already fun when something unexpected happens. The staging of errors that make the automaton seem human, the unusual sounds, the friction in the gears, getting tangled up in the gestures—all of that could be interpreted as fun. For me, these are necessities, because I fear a well-oiled machine—and thus the predictable. And perhaps also I can’t take things, or myself, too seriously. So there may, after all, be a certain humorous distance, and therefore an unconscious influence on the tracks. But as the author myself, I can’t hear it. And that means humor would not have a defined role right now. If anything, it just happens, as it does in encounters with other people. For me, humor is indispensable there. In any case, I want to keep thinking about your question. There are quite a few inspiring examples in music, but also in visual art, that I would definitely describe as humorous. And maybe humor can get a more definite role in my work too. ACL: Thank you very much for your time, Sven. Is there anything else you’d like to tell our readers before closing this interview? EO: I’d like to thank you for these really challenging and intense questions. They went quite deep, and I found it very inspiring to think about them. Now I’m curious to know what it’s like to listen to the album after reading this interview—how it affects the way we perceive and contextualize this music. Especially since the album doesn’t necessarily need a strong conceptual framework, as it was created largely intuitively. Talking about it this way now almost feels like a kind of mental post-production, even though the music is already finished. And I consider it something special in itself to be able to release music like this, in the hope that there will be a few people out there who will actually listen to it and perhaps even find something in it. Thanks again for this opportunity.

An instant soundtrack to your inner movie, or your outer one OBA by OBA   Power up the hi-fi and get your favorite seventies era Sci-Fi laserdisc movie cued up on your vintage home entertainment system, turn the volume down on the film, and turn up the volume on OBA to let them provide the soundtrack. Turning the TV down and the stereo up is something old headz used to do. Out pattern making tendencies will find parallels with the visuals on the tube and the sounds from the music matching up in eerie ways. Look how far this took the acid addled minds of people who did this with the Wizard of Oz and the Dark Side of the Moon! OBA has provided an instant soundtrack to your inner movie, or your outer one. The project got started when three friends from three different continents found themselves in the same place and made a recording session, as musical friends are wont to do. The frequency wizard Amir Khay Nir from the USA, had met up with Orri Dror from Iceland, and Benjamin Esterlis in Israel. All of these fellows are multi-instrumentalists, making this an outing in overdubs after the initial recordings. But it is so freaking solid you think it was all happening live, and that’s the beauty of the recorded medium. It can make a live band out of a trio who live in far flung corners of the world. When I hear this music, I can see them playing, even it was completed after the initial sessions, and even if I don’t know what any of them look like. Synth’s swoon around drums, guitar and bass from the opening tones in an energetic weave. Not long after opening on “Ptaltalim” it starts to sound like a blurred VHS tape with bad tracking, but just for a second. The edited imperfection makes you awake to the perfection of the music, all moving into an action packed, almost aggressive soundscape of tight knit interlinking rhythms. What stands out: Intertwined souls: The chords and melodies played here make you know that you are listening to a group of people who are at ease musically syncing to each other despite the normal distances that separate them on the globe. We hear how the bass and guitar dialogues in pleasure with percolating synth, and whispers of flute as they paint the air and space and space with sound in a mood of sonic freedom. Emotional narrative: Though there is no voice and there are no lyrics in this entirely instrumental album, it moves naturally along an arc of action, reverie, intimation, and release across seven songs. It’s a soundtrack, but you make up the movie in your head. Chromatic resonance: From the melancholic power of “Luna Gal” to the electro-baroque impressionism of “Ketem” and progressive passages reminiscent of long time favorites such as Klaus Schulze, the album progresses like a well-structured musical short story (it’s a short and concise album) even as it permutates along the lines of something out of the studio of Gottfried Michael Koenig. Calculated chaos: All the notes are in the right place, and though there are a lot of notes, it’s not about showing off virtuosity. The skill of the players is in service to each composition. It’s a sincere work paying homage to classic forms, showing those forms are just as exciting when made anew. A touch of acid: Psychedelic inspiration is prominent throughout this work which invites dark room, eyes closed, introspective listening for out of body time. New listens reveal new textures, emotion and the craftsmanship that goes with attention to detail. OBA is available on Schwarz Neon Licht. items.body: The Dexadream seems to soar hundreds of miles above our atmosphere, while DFTSKZ-V333 drifts in and out of downtempo electronic bubbles of sound and space, funk, and textural, beat-laden wonders. Across both releases, Xurba folds left-field elements into a language entirely his own, shaping sound into something hazy, distant, and quietly otherworldly.   Suspended somewhere between memory and imagination A hauntological layer drifts through both DFTSKZ-V333 and The Dexadream, as elongated, slowly evolving loops—dark, buried, and scorched with abstraction—sees longtime fuzzy electronic sonic sculptor Will Brazier-Smith (aka Xurba) continuing to push ambient time capsules into unfamiliar territory. Where DFTSKZ-V333 settles into darker ambient motifs punctuated by subtle percussive bleeps, The Dexadream lifts that same hazy sensibility into a more expansive space, with atmosphere and downtempo noise conjuring a sense of nostalgic bewilderment. Much like the peculiar, roughened soundtracks of Pentagrams Of Discordia, Xurba blends, refines, and accents fragments into dreamlike ambient worlds that feel suspended somewhere between memory and imagination. The Dexadream seems to soar hundreds of miles above our atmosphere, while DFTSKZ-V333 hovers near terra firma—weaving in and out of downtempo electronic bubbles of sound and space, funk, and textural, beat-laden wonders. Across both releases, Xurba folds left-field elements into a language entirely his own, shaping sound into something hazy, distant, and quietly otherworldly. DFTSKZ-V333 & DFTSKZ-V333 EP’s are available on Electric Studios. items.body: In a world increasingly obsessed with acceleration, Ekzon offers something altogether more radical—the opportunity to pause, listen, and feel the architecture of the moment dissolve gently into light. Spaces you can inhabit rather than simply observe Ambient Series Volume 2 by Ekzon   Ekzon maintains his high-calibre, sophisticated corner of sound and rhythmic creation with the stunning self-released Ambient Series Volume 2. Throughout my experience of ambient music’s more spacious possibilities, I have remained resolutely attached to the seminal 76:14 by Global Communication: another timestamp, and one of the first truly compelling ambient albums to emerge in the wake of The Orb‘s The Orb’s Adventures Beyond the Ultraworld, itself part of a lineage stretching back to Brian Eno‘s earliest explorations of spatial, aural atmosphere in Music for AIrports—these that became the seed of decades of an entire genre and beyond. This history lends some sense of the gravitas from which Ekzon operates—and perhaps unknowingly continues—in his own experiments with atmosphere as the leading texture. Already a deft hand at next-level rhythmic, programmatic glitch and electro-adjacent finery, this second collection extends those ideas across twelve tender pieces articulating contemporary urban life—not as a cold technological landscape, but as something lived within, felt through and quietly transformed by human presence. “Throughout all 12 pieces, multi-timbral pads drift through peaks and troughs of rhythmic puncture and oceanic blooms of turquoise transcendence.” ~Will Dawkins Titles and temperatures such as “Inertial Dream,” “A Quiet Ascent,” “Fading Echoes” and “City Lights” frame a subjective, phenomenological view of contemporary advancement, while the immediately captivating “Machines, Men, and Nature” feels almost like a small manifesto: a reconciliation of the organic and synthetic, the constructed and the instinctive. There is a generosity here, a willingness to let sound breathe rather than constantly announce itself. Throughout all 12 pieces, multi-timbral pads drift through peaks and troughs of rhythmic puncture and oceanic blooms of turquoise transcendence. Figurative angels seem to circle somewhere within the mix, gently worrying at the heartstrings without ever slipping into sentimentality. At times there are beats to grasp and solidify; at others, only clear air, the scent of magnolia, and beautiful collisions of earnest intention. The feeling of pragmatic melancholy that endures after the almost static movement in the exquisite “Twilight Water” is a not to be missed experience. Just stunning. Closing titles duties goes to the sublime “Crystallised” a breathtaking pulse of warm fogged out bliss in motion. Finally, for me, what makes Ambient Series V2 especially compelling, and adjacent to the aforementioned classics is its sense of unremitting balance, its relationship to its desire to be expressed. Ekzon understands that atmosphere need not mean inertia, and that sophistication need not sacrifice its correlation to necessary warmth. These tracks are spaces you can inhabit rather than simply observe: quietly detailed, emotionally open and touched by a rare sense of profound possibility. In a world increasingly obsessed with acceleration, Ekzon offers something altogether more radical—the opportunity to pause, listen, and feel the architecture of the moment dissolve gently into light. Ambient Series Volume 2 is available on Bandcamp. [ekzon.fr] Ambient Series Volume 2 by Ekzon  The post Ekzon :: Ambient Series Volume 2 (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Expanding rather than merging the recognized individual styles of each, Fictions results in a chronostatic set of pieces with error honored as a hidden intention (see Eno’s Oblique Strategies) via analog processes, while holding to melodic virtues and economy of means. Languorous veiled melodies choreographed into an immersive suite Fictions by Lamasz & Grandbruit   Following release in early July, Fictions, somewhat mirroring its own dynamic, has taken time to reach peak resonance, creeping via auditory channels into psychoactive life, effectively bringing together the defining elements of each of Lamasz and Grandbruit into a single body of work. The return to Past Inside the Present of Pierre Luc (Lamasz) and Francis Tremblay (Grandbruit) with this collaboration comes on the back of four solo releases across the label: Fictions draws on Nature Morte (2020) and Broderie (2021) in tape loop-driven nature, Ruptures (2020) and Ville inerte (2021) in use of stratified guitar and environmental sound, common ground found in manicured noise, overall ambience and recursive habit. The brothers allow a gradual evolution, pieces looping into processed guitar-smeared harmonic tracts, tape hiss effectively taking on an active compositional role transcending background color. Expanding rather than merging the recognized individual styles of each, Fictions results in a chronostatic set of pieces with error honored as a hidden intention (see Eno’s Oblique Strategies) via analog processes, while holding to melodic virtues and economy of means. Fictions, then, adds to both artists’ growing back catalog, with languorous veiled melodies choreographed into an immersive suite with an emotional heft matching its timbral resonance. RIYL Chihei Hatakeyama, Rafael Anton Irisarri and artists in adjacent zones. Fictions is out available on Past Inside the Present [Bandcamp] Fictions by Lamasz & GrandbruitThe post Lamasz & Grandbruit :: Fictions (Past Inside the Present) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Melodic gestures emerge from drone surrounds—ground to figure, dissolving into field—drawing you in from perception’s margins, receding just as they seem to have settled. A platform to explore themes of presence, absence, removal and acceptance Disappear in Silent Ways by Halftribe   At the intersection of ambient, drone and environmental sound you’ll find Halftribe. His return to Dronarivm, Disappear in Silent Ways, comes in colors at once luminous and blurred, with a captivating ambi[val]ence, evoking a sense of moments presenting with past inside. Evanescence. This is achieved partly via a keen melodic sensibility with soft analog-y synths, field captures and odd voice fragments crafted into tone poems at once expansive and intimate. A form of minimalism runs through DiSW, manifest not in ideological stance but simple compositional practice; Ryan Bissett eschews the impulse for new entries to the sound stage for letting sounds evolve, adding color to broader canvas before letting in other elements. Sounds recede then return, revenant—a vague sense of movement over overt development; a soft ebb-flow dynamic, harmonic shifts emerging to color tenor, drones privileging depth over density, minute tonal shifts reframing space around and within. Melodic gestures emerge from drone surrounds—ground to figure, dissolving into field—drawing you in from perception’s margins, receding just as they seem to have settled. A site of refuge found after disappearing :: “Listen,” bids us attend to our environs, with its leitmotif ‘what we listen to is constantly feeding us’ adjuring mindfulness of what we let in. Field recordings bring in the natural world, as on “Dusk,” mixing layered drones with rainfall, evoking crepuscular horizons in day-night transition, inner-outer boundaries dissolved; or “Sanctuary,” pointing to a site of refuge found after disappearing; its oneiric mood feeds into “Yearn,” water flow enhancing a sense of peace through nature connection. “Windfall” shifts focus from water, distant whispers suggesting a field with grass and trees windblown, light filtering through branches to slow cloud drift. The title track brings an interlude of release, with birdsong and babbling before “Everything Comes to an End” leaves us with… that sense of evanescence. Following For the Summer, or Forever (2018) and Elegant, Golden (2022), Dronarivm has provided Halftribe with a platform to explore themes of presence, absence, removal and acceptance. The artist’s stamp, though, is more outline than full imprint, DiSW not looking to thematic statement so much as documenting the resonance of a feeling, in all its contours. items.body: Dudamel Conducts Prokofiev, Adams & Di Castri A visceral work headlined the opening program of the NY Philharmonic’s 2026-2027 season at Geffen Hall at Lincoln Center on September 16: John Adams’ On the Transmigration of Souls, a work written in response to the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center. As the 25th anniversary of the tragedy was just a few days prior, my gut was still tender from the echoes of the memories of that day. The work included a recording on which the names of some of the victims were spoken. Even a quarter century later, hearing the names put me right into that somber feeling I had experienced last week. The work effectively conveyed the desperation, shock and numbness, grief and sadness of those days. In a way, the orchestra provided a soundtrack for this actuality, and the overall effect was mystical, otherworldly and deeply affecting. At the conclusion, an exceptionally long “hang time” of silence hung over the concert hall – even after conductor Gustavo Dudamel lowered his arms, a visual signal that the piece was over, the audience stayed quiet, giving a bit of contemplative quiet before the roaring applause. I didn’t feel like hearing anything else after that – I just wanted to go to a bar and have a stiff drink. I was curious how the next piece, a world premiere by Zosha Di Castri, would land directly after the emotional tension of the Adams piece. Di Castri’s Invisible House — co-commissioned by the Philharmonic — opened with low brass and bass, a rumble that I felt in my chest. The Philharmonic’s brass had a starring role here, and the entire section sounded brilliant. The piece felt a little unfocused, although that could have been me — my head was still occupied with the sounds and emotions of Transmigration of Souls. The program closed with Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5, and on this more familiar ground it was apparent how utterly terrific the Philharmonic sounded. Timbres of the various orchestral sections blended beautifully – achieving a very well-balanced sound. The symphony’s dark undercurrent showed off the winds especially well. Gustavo Dudamel‘s energetic conducting style was entertaining to watch as his entire body twitched and convulsed in the bombastic sections. In this concert, the New York Philharmonic sounded as good, and as present, as I’ve ever heard them. Finally, four years after Geffen Hall’s renovation, the orchestra has settled into the hall, and the hall has wrapped itself around the orchestra. Both the band and the space have gotten used to each other and found ways to work together as a single organism. The post John Adams’ “On the Transmigration of Souls” – A Visceral Experience appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Ska and rocksteady set the tempo on “Be Who You Are”, a faster footing than the roots rhythms Macka B ordinarily records over, and he toasts across it in the measured address that has defined his delivery since the early 1980s. The single was released on 21 August, composed and produced by the Hamburg musician Paul Lupa, who plays keyboards and bass and surrounds them with a live rhythm section: Big Finga on drums, Robert “Dubwise” Browne on guitar, Tribuman on horns. The horns carry the melodic line, the guitar marks the offbeat, and the vocal sits forward in the mix, with the phrasing of a lyric Macka B wrote himself, vocal melody included. What he tells the listener is to be who they are. Advice has been his line of work for forty years. He has been called “the Teacher” since the 1980s for songs about what to eat, how to look after yourself and how to treat other people, and the Wha Me Eat Wednesdays vegan raps he began posting in 2017 carried that voice far beyond the reggae circuit. Lupa has been building his Hamburg catalogue around Jamaican and German vocalists since 2022, and Macka B is the most established voice to record over one of his rhythms so far. items.body: “Yira Ye” takes its title from a Bambara phrase that means roughly “that’s how it is”, and it is the first single from L’Ombre du Croco, the debut album  Bamako Express release through Trad Records on 30 October. The Ghent quartet pairs two Belgian folk players, violinist Anouk Sanczuk and guitarist Florian De Schepper, with Malian balafonist and singer Joël Massa Diarra and Burkinabè percussionist Ousmane Dembélé on djembe and calabash. Their songs are sung in Bambara. Over the past year they have played concert stages and the balfolk nights of Flanders, where couples dance to live folk bands, and in 2026 they won Best Live Band at the Flanders Folk Awards. At a balfolk night the violin carries the tune for the dancers, and in Mande music the balafon does much the same job; “Yira Ye” passes the melody between the two over Dembélé’s djembe. The track moves from quiet melodic passages into full dance rhythm, and De Schepper steps forward for a guitar solo, recorded with the rest of the song by Jeroen Geerinck at Studio Trad. items.body: Ministry released “Singularity” on September 18, 2026 through Cleopatra Records, the third single from the industrial band’s final studio album, “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)“, due October 30. The track follows the earlier singles “Burned Out” and “We Hate” from the same record. “Singularity” takes on artificial intelligence, built around a warning voiced by a cyborg character: “Your time on this planet has passed […] we are in control.” A press release ties the song to recent public alarm over AI, describing it as Al Jourgensen and the band’s timely take on the subject. The music video was directed by Ben Garcia of Rage4Order Designs, working with Jourgensen and Joshua Bradford, a former Revolting Cocks bandmate who also directed the videos for “Burned Out” and “We Hate.” Where ‘Singularity’ sits on ‘Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)’ “Singularity” is track eight of ten. The album closes with “We’re Still Here”, the only track to feature former Ministry bassist Paul Barker, alongside the band’s current lineup of guitarists Monte Pittman and Cesar Soto, bassist Paul D’Amour, sampler and synth player John Bechdel, and drummer Pepe Clarke Magaña. “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)” arrives on vinyl, CD, cassette and digital formats, plus four vinyl variants (Green & Black Splatter, Silver & Black Splatter and Coke Bottle Green LPs) and two box sets pairing a splatter or marble LP with a picture LP, 7-inch and CD. Track seven, “The White Man Lied”, is left off the cassette and vinyl pressings. The full tracklist reads: Crickets Voices of Hate Clown Car We Hate Delete Grifter The White Man Lied Singularity Burned Out We’re Still Here (feat. Paul Barker) The album is available for preorder through Cleopatra Records. Ministry ‘Goodbye Europe’ tour dates 2027 Ministry closes out its career with a farewell touring cycle. Before the European leg, the band plays its remaining 2026 US and international dates: September 20 at Louder Than Life in Louisville, October 3 at the Salt Shed in Chicago, and October 24 at Sick New World Texas in Fort Worth, followed by Australia’s Good Things Festival in December with new side shows in Sydney and Adelaide. The “Goodbye Europe” tour, with Die Krupps as special guests, opens in Utrecht on April 2, 2027 and closes in Helsinki on May 1: April 2, 2027 – Utrecht, Netherlands April 3, 2027 – Saarbrücken, Germany April 4, 2027 – Brussels, Belgium April 6, 2027 – Manchester, UK April 7, 2027 – Dublin, Ireland April 9, 2027 – Nottingham, UK April 10, 2027 – London, UK April 12, 2027 – Paris, France April 14, 2027 – Madrid, Spain April 15, 2027 – Barcelona, Spain April 17, 2027 – Lausanne, Switzerland April 18, 2027 – Munich, Germany April 19, 2027 – Vienna, Austria April 21, 2027 – Prague, Czech Republic April 22, 2027 – Warsaw, Poland April 24, 2027 – Berlin, Germany April 25, 2027 – Hamburg, Germany April 26, 2027 – Copenhagen, Denmark April 27, 2027 – Oslo, Norway April 29, 2027 – Stockholm, Sweden May 1, 2027 – Helsinki, Finland A full US leg of the farewell tour has not yet been announced. About Ministry Ministry was formed in Chicago in 1981 by Al Jourgensen, a pioneering figure in industrial music. The project started with synth-pop material issued as four 12-inch singles on the newly founded Wax Trax! Records before the debut album “With Sympathy” on Arista Records in 1983. Jourgensen moved the band toward a harsher, sample-driven sound across “Twitch” (1986), “The Land of Rape and Honey” (1988) and “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste” (1989), then reached its widest audience with “Psalm 69: The Way to Succeed and the Way to Suck Eggs” (1992), which brought the first of six Grammy nominations. Paul Barker played bass and co-produced through that period before leaving the band in 2003. Eight further albums followed before Jourgensen shut the band down in 2013. Ministry returned in 2018 with “AmeriKKKant”, then issued “Moral Hygiene” (2021) and “HOPIUMFORTHEMASSES” (2024), its 16th studio album. In March 2025 the band released “The Squirrely Years Revisited” on Cleopatra Records, a set of re-recorded songs from its early synth-pop catalogue, and followed it with first-ever official videos for “Everyday Is Halloween” and “I’ll Do Anything For You” and a Jurgen Engler remix of the live track “Dancing Alone” in March 2026. Alongside Ministry, Jourgensen has run Revolting Cocks, Lard, Pailhead and Surgical Meth Machine; Barker returned to recording as Lead Into Gold in 2023. Across 45 years, Ministry has released 17 studio albums, 8 live releases and 8 side projects, toured five continents, and published an autobiography and two documentaries. “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)” closes that catalogue as the band’s final album, and “Singularity” is its third single.

items.body: US goth-industrial artist EVA X released the single “Dance in Shadows” on 18 September 2026, alongside the announcement of her second album, “TURBOPINK”, due 6 November. The single mixes synthpop, metal, power pop and 80s-referencing production, and comes backed with a breakbeat remix by Stoneburner. “Dance in Shadows” was written by EVA X collaborator Gaby Gustafson after a co-worker and friend died of an aggressive form of cancer. “I had written a super sad song originally, but I knew she’d hate that. It was really important to her to find joy wherever she could. So I ended up reworking the track into Dance in Shadows, our happy little song about death,” Gustafson stated. The B-side carries a breakbeat remix of the track by Stoneburner. EVA X’s ‘TURBOPINK’ album due 6 November “TURBOPINK” follows EVA X’s debut album, “I Dream of a Reality”, released on Distortion Productions in 2022. “Dance in Shadows” serves as the album’s preview single. EVA X returns with a full band for the touring cycle around the new record. About EVA X EVA X began as a bedroom producer, releasing her first tracks in 2019 and building a following in the goth and industrial scene through a fusion of synthwave, industrial, power pop and metal elements. Her debut album, “I Dream of a Reality”, came out on Distortion Productions in 2022 and appeared on several “best of 2022” year-end lists. She has performed at New Jersey’s Dark Force Fest, Seattle’s Mechanismus Festival and Calgary’s Terminus. Side-Line previously covered her single and video “Dopamine Blind” (2024) and her video “Machine” (2021). With “Dance in Shadows”, EVA X previews her second album, “TURBOPINK”, out 6 November 2026.

items.body: US goth-pop project Metamorph released the single “Witchfire” and its official video on 18 September 2026. The track is produced by Erik Gustafson and pairs dance-oriented beats with hook-driven melodies, alongside an extended dance mix featuring a flute solo from vocalist Margot Day. The “Witchfire” video was filmed by Brian Wimer in New York’s East Village, where Margot Day lived and performed with The Plague in the 1980s, and in the forests of Vermont. It features Day alongside bandmate Kurtis Knight. The extended dance mix, which includes Day’s flute solo, will get its own video at a later date. Metamorph’s release history Metamorph is the project of Margot Day, a New York vocalist, flutist and songwriter who fronted The Plague during the 1980s NYC goth scene alongside drummers Nick Ferrell (Spahn Ranch) and Damian (Misfits). Earlier in her career, Day played in Slow Walk 13 alongside Adam Yauch of the Beastie Boys. Formed in 2016, Metamorph blends gothic atmosphere, dark synth textures and pop songwriting built around Day’s vocals and flute playing, with Kurtis Knight providing dark synths and backing vocals on stage. Metamorph’s back catalogue includes the album “Kiss of the Witch” (2022), the album “Hex” (2024) and the retrospective “Haunted Hearts XIII” (2025), all produced by Erik Gustafson. The project has released remixes by Leaether Strip and Assemblage 23, and the single “Dance of a 1000 Miracles” featuring Stabbing Westward‘s Chris Hall has passed 20,000 Spotify streams. Metamorph has performed across the United States, Canada, Costa Rica and Guatemala, with music videos totalling more than 250,000 YouTube views. “Witchfire” follows Metamorph’s 2025 EP “Harlot” on Distortion Productions.

items.body: Nick Rhodes of Duran Duran produced Wendy Bevan’s new single “Sleepwalkers,” the third preview of the UK goth electro-pop artist’s album “Alone With The Unknown,” due September 18. The track pairs Bevan’s vocals with atmospheric synthesizer arrangements built around a feeling of loss without a clean goodbye, leaving the listener suspended between holding on and letting go. Bevan describes “Sleepwalkers” as a piece about two sides of the same uncertainty: “the old world that’s disappeared and the future that hasn’t arrived.” “We’re left somewhere, timeless and in between,” she said. “Sometimes we become so lost in our own dreams that we don’t see the destruction they cause, or recognize that we may be disappearing from our own lives.” On the song’s central tension, she added: “The act of not choosing can be just as violent as a bull in a china shop. While we long for a place called home, we unconsciously fill the spaces between with our own self-destructive behaviors.” “Sleepwalkers” is track nine on “Alone With The Unknown,” out September 18 on Chiaroscuro. The 13-track album, which also carries the bonus cut “Crazy Kinda Feeling,” was preceded by the singles “Innocence” in July and “Fragile Times” in August, both also produced by Nick Rhodes. The record continues Bevan’s production partnership with Rhodes, which began with the instrumental Astronomia series. About Wendy Bevan Wendy Bevan is a British singer, violinist and photographer raised in London who now lives in Los Angeles. She released the single “Love from the Moon” via Unknown Pleasures Records in 2016, alongside a parallel career as a fashion and fine-art photographer. In 2018 she began collaborating with Duran Duran’s Nick Rhodes, working between Los Angeles and London, on a series of cinematic instrumental compositions released from 2021 as the Astronomia project through Tape Modern, the label founded by Stephen Duffy and Nick Rhodes. The series opened with “The Fall of Saturn” on the spring equinox of 2021, followed by “Astronomia II: The Rise of Lyra” that June. In October 2024, Bevan released “Chromesthesia,” a five-track instrumental album, through her own Bandcamp page. She and Rhodes then returned to song-based material for “Alone With The Unknown,” due September 18, with “Sleepwalkers” as its third single.

items.body: Ghost Reflection, the dark electro and industrial project of Alexander Borsov, releases the concept album “Dark Triad” digitally on Aliens Production. The eight-track record mixes melodic lines, IDM loops and analog electronics around a horror-themed narrative. Borsov wrote, produced, designed and mastered “Dark Triad” himself. Aliens Production describes the record as “a cinematic concept rooted in horror aesthetics and rhythmic themes.” The tracklist runs “Games of psychopaths,” “Dark Triad,” “Integration of Madness,” “Infected,” “The root of evil,” “Thorny path,” “The Shattered World of Illusions” and “Order of Darkness.” Dark Triad by Ghost Reflection Ghost Reflection’s ‘Dark Triad’ concept The eight tracks move from “Games of psychopaths” through “Integration of Madness” and “The root of evil” to the closing “Order of Darkness,” a sequence built around horror imagery and rhythmic industrial and IDM production rather than a conventional song structure. “Dark Triad” first appeared under Borsov’s own Bandcamp page in September 2025 and now returns through Aliens Production as a digital release. About Ghost Reflection Ghost Reflection is one of several recording names used by Slovak producer Alexander Borsov, alongside Dark the Keeper, Darkmechanic and Stellar Dynamics, all mixing electro-industrial, noise and horror-themed dark electro elements. Borsov is also a member of the group Diverje and got his start in metal bands including Morgue, Atom, Cremation Deads, Sarcoma and Satura before moving into electronic production. Under the Ghost Reflection name, Borsov released the album “Dark Thinker” in June 2022 and the single “Dark Noise” in February 2024. “Dark Triad” followed in September 2025 and is now released digitally through Aliens Production, the Slovak dark electronics label that has operated since 1997 and hosts a roster of industrial, dark electro and EBM-adjacent acts.

items.body: Union Chapel in London stages “Vinyl Requiem 33.3” on 4 November 2026, a one-off return of Philip Jeck and Lol Sargent’s “Vinyl Requiem” to the venue where it premiered in 1993. Doors open at 18:30 and the programme starts at 19:30. Tickets are £18 plus booking fee through gigantic.com and are on sale now. The evening also marks the launch of a limited-edition double-vinyl reissue of “Vinyl Requiem” on Touch, the label Jeck was signed to from 1995 until his death in 2022. Vinyl Requiem 33.3 event details The programme centres on a full-scale projection of the 55-minute edited film of the 1993 performance, followed by a Q&A with people connected to the work and to Jeck’s creative life: Ghislaine Boddington (artistic director of the arts collective shinkansen), Mary Prestidge and Lol Sargent, the visual artist who created “Vinyl Requiem” with Jeck. Jon Wozencroft, co-founder of Touch, is also billed to take part. All profits from the night go to The Philip Jeck Foundation, a charity set up by Jeck’s family after his death to fund artists who produce experimental and creative work. Conceived by Jeck and Sargent at the start of the 1990s under the working title “The Death of Vinyl”, “Vinyl Requiem” was built for the 1993 Union Chapel performance from an 8-by-6-metre wall of 180 white Dansette record players, combined with 9 slide projectors and 2 16mm film projectors, according to Touch’s own catalogue notes. Three “Dansette operators” walked platforms in front of the record-player wall to swap discs live during the piece. The 1993 premiere was staged with the Institute of Contemporary Arts and also travelled to Ghent’s Time Festival in Belgium, later touring the UK, Austria and Belgium with support from the Arts Council. It won the Time Out Performance Award for Best Site-Specific Event in 1993. Sargent described the piece’s intent in an interview given around the time of its 20th anniversary: “What Philip and I created was an abstract expressionistic performance made in a very intuitive way to celebrate over 100 years of the mass public experience of the ‘record’. It was an art installation performance about a medium, using the medium.” Jeck, discussing the same period, was careful to separate the piece from nostalgia: “[Vinyl Requiem was not] a big mourning for records, I am not anti CD. It is a good starting point to mark this time of change from vinyl to other formats.” He also drew a direct line between his own practice and Sargent’s: “Lol uses his computer-controlled projectors as paint brushes. He paints with light which is similar to the way that I work with sound.” The critic David Toop, writing about the piece at the time, described its atmosphere in a short, often-cited line: “a mood of poignancy. Perhaps sadness is intrinsic to the medium.” About Philip Jeck and Lol Sargent Philip Jeck was born on 15 November 1952 and studied visual arts at Dartington College of Arts in Devon. After a trip to New York in 1979 introduced him to DJs including Walter Gibbons and Larry Levan, he began building compositions from old record players and vinyl in the early 1980s, initially scoring work for dance and theatre companies, including a five-year collaboration with choreographer Laurie Booth. “Vinyl Requiem”, made with Sargent for the 1993 Union Chapel performance, became his best-known work. Jeck signed to Touch in 1995 and released a run of albums on the label including “Loopholes” (1995), “Surf” (1998), “Stoke” (2002), “7” (2003), “Sand” (2008), “An Ark for the Listener” (2010) and “Cardinal” (2015). “Sand” was named the second-best album of 2008 by The Wire. He received the Paul Hamlyn Foundation Award for Composers in 2009. Jeck also collaborated with Jah Wobble, Jaki Liebezeit, David Sylvian, Janek Schaefer and Gavin Bryars, among others; his final credited recording was “Stardust”, a 2021 collaboration with Faith Coloccia. He died on 25 March 2022 in Liverpool, aged 69, following a brief illness. His family, including Mary Prestidge, subsequently established The Philip Jeck Foundation in his name. Lol Sargent is a UK visual artist who worked with Jeck on “Vinyl Requiem” from its conception, designing and hand-triggering the piece’s slide and film projections during live performances. He later oversaw the archival 55-minute edit of the 1993 film, released on DVD in 2013 with all proceeds going to The Philip Jeck Foundation. “Vinyl Requiem 33.3” reunites Sargent with the venue, the film and several of the people who worked on the original production, alongside the new Touch double-vinyl reissue of “Vinyl Requiem”.

items.body: Unter Strøm, the electronic duo of Alex Gonzales (Matte Blvck) and John Kunkel (The New Division, John Grand), release Transmission 003: Live at the Breathing Records Showcase, an independent live recording that runs a little over 84 minutes. The set documents a full Unter Strøm performance at a Breathing Records showcase and includes live versions of “Fragment” and “Stumbling” performed before either track had been released, along with several vocal tracks the duo were still developing. Unlike the project’s prior singles, “Transmission 003” is not a studio release. It is a concert recording, filmed and uploaded to YouTube, capturing the duo’s first time performing an Unter Strøm set in front of an audience. Unter Strøm test unreleased material in a live setting The showcase gave Gonzales and Kunkel their first chance to hear the project’s unreleased catalog through a full sound system and gauge a crowd’s reaction to it in real time. Kunkel described the goal behind the set: “We wanted the set to present a broad landscape of the Unter Strøm sound and show how many different places the project can go. After working on this music for over a year, it was exciting to finally experience it through a proper sound system and watch people respond to it in real time. What makes it even more exciting is that we still have a lot more in the tank that didn’t make it into the set.” Gonzales, describing what the performance meant for the duo, added: “The Breathing Records showcase was the first time we played an Unter Strøm set in front of an audience, so it felt like an important moment for us. We performed an hour and a half of entirely unreleased material, including ‘Fragment’ and ‘Stumbling’ before either song had been released, as well as several vocal tracks that we were still developing. It gave us a rare opportunity to test this body of work in a live environment and see which moments connected instinctively with the audience.” About Unter Strøm Unter Strøm is an electronic duo formed by Alex Gonzales and John Kunkel, based between Los Angeles and San Diego after years of the pair working together in earlier bands and studio sessions. The project mixes techno, melodic house and industrial electronics. Gonzales also records as Matte Blvck, the San Diego-based darkwave and industrial trio he leads with Bidi Cobra and Daniel Corrales, whose releases include “Vows,” “Pupula Duplex” and “Soulless.” Kunkel is the Los Angeles-based producer and songwriter behind The New Division, the synth-pop project he has led since the 2000s, is part of the Los Angeles group Trade Secrets, and also produces melodic house as John Grand, an alias that has appeared on Armin van Buuren’s A State of Trance and on Above & Beyond’s Group Therapy Radio. Unter Strøm debuted in 2025 with the two-track single “Breathing” before signing to Breathing Records, the label that launched with the “Inhale Vol. I” compilation in November 2025. The duo then released “Orynth” on May 15, 2026, “Fold” on June 12, 2026, “Fragment” on July 24, 2026 and “Stumbling” on August 28, 2026, the four singles that made up the “Between Forms” run. “Transmission 003: Live at the Breathing Records Showcase” now documents the live set where “Fragment” and “Stumbling” were first performed, ahead of their studio releases, alongside new vocal material the duo have yet to put out.

items.body: French print fanzine Lumières Noires has released its third issue, “Lumières Noires Fanzine N°3”, out now on Bandcamp. The zine is founded and edited by Vincent Dromard and covers underground and dark music. Printed in a run of 104 hand-numbered copies, the issue comes in A5 format with a glossy hardcover, 124 pages in color and black-and-white, perfect-bound and digitally printed. The text is in French. Lumières Noires Fanzine N°3 covers Pharmakon (harsh noise, visceral industrial – USA), Rosemary Loves A Blackberry / Diana Burkot (electronic art pop – Iceland/Russia), Jennifer Touch (dark acidwave – Germany), Ailise Blake (cosmic neofolk – Italy/France), Dermabrasion (death rock, disco punk – Canada), Madeline Goldstein (wet new wave – USA), Hilary Woods (blinding black drone folk – Ireland) and Robin Kester (psychedelic pop, electro rock – Netherlands), plus Buzzkill (coldwave, steel-hard punk – France), along with more than fifty reviews of vinyl, CD, cassette and VHS releases. Dromard, who runs the fanzine from France, described the issue as dedicated “to underground music.” About Lumières Noires Fanzine Lumières Noires is a French print fanzine covering underground and dark music, founded and edited by Vincent Dromard. Its first issue was released in March 2025 after six months of work, printed in 108 hand-numbered copies: A5 format, glossy hardcover, 112 pages in color and black-and-white, perfect-bound and digitally printed. That issue included interviews and features on artists such as Kælan Mikla and Denuit, alongside about fifty reviews of physical releases. The second issue followed around November 2025, printed in 100 hand-numbered copies in the same A5 glossy hardcover format, 116 pages in color and black-and-white, perfect-bound and digitally printed. It featured Ic3peak, Left For Pleasure, Donna Blue, Systeme Paradoxe, Blanche Biau, Dlina Volny, Babel Map, La Punta Bianca and Violent Vickie, plus fifty-four reviews of vinyl, CD, cassette and DVD releases; each order included a 40×30 cm poster. Lumières Noires Fanzine N°3, released in September 2026, is the third issue since the zine launched, and is available on Bandcamp alongside the first two.

items.body: The 21st-anniversary triple-vinyl reissue of Andy Bell’s “Electric Blue” has a new release date of December 4, 2026, according to the Erasure Information Service newsletter sent to subscribers on September 18, 2026. The accompanying 12″ vinyl single, “Love Oneself” / “Delicious”, is now scheduled for November 20, 2026. The Andy Bell reissue was previously delayed after audio issues were found in the test pressings. Newsletter editor Richard Evans wrote that the issues have since been corrected, new test pressings are due shortly, and the release has been rebooked into the pressing plant’s production queue. Stock delivered ahead of the release date will be dispatched to fulfil pre-orders as soon as it arrives. Everyone who has pre-ordered Andy Bell’s “Electric Blue” through Lexer Music will receive an MP3 version of the album while they wait, an offer that also applies to pre-orders placed via Lexer before September 28, 2026. The same MP3 offer applies to pre-orders of the “Love Oneself” / “Delicious” 12″ single. Vince Clarke contributes to new Ultravox book The same newsletter carries a mention of Vince Clarke‘s contribution to “Looking Backwards Towards The Future: The Story of Ultravox”, a book by Richard Evans due out on October 8, 2026 everywhere except North America, Australia and New Zealand, where it follows in February. Clarke was interviewed for the book about his fondness for Ultravox‘s “Systems Of Romance” album. The book is written with the cooperation of Ultravox’s surviving core members, carries a foreword by Moby, and includes additional contributions from Duran Duran’s Nick Rhodes and producer Steve Lillywhite. Signed and dedicated copies are available to order through Lexer Music. Unofficial remix and a teased new chapter The newsletter also points to a new unofficial remix of Erasure’s “Stay With Me” by an artist called Klaak, posted to YouTube, following an earlier unofficial Klaak remix of “Hideaway”. The remix is not sanctioned by Erasure, Andy Bell or Mute. Evans also teased that preparations are underway to announce “the next exciting chapter in Erasure’s story,” tied to a forthcoming new Erasure album project. About Erasure and Andy Bell Erasure are the English synth-pop duo of Andy Bell and Vince Clarke, formed in London in 1985. Clarke had previously co-founded Depeche Mode and Yazoo, and formed The Assembly, before pairing with vocalist Bell to form Erasure. The duo built a run of UK and international hits through the late 1980s and 1990s, including “Sometimes,” “A Little Respect,” “Chains of Love,” “Blue Savannah” and “Always.” Erasure’s catalogue has been the subject of ongoing reissue campaigns, including a 2024 vinyl reissue push covering ‘Tomorrow’s World’, ‘Snow Globe’ and ‘The Violet Flame’, and the duo marked 40 years of “Who Needs Love Like That” in 2025. Bell has maintained a solo career alongside Erasure, releasing the album “Ten Crowns” in 2025 and continuing to perform and record under his own name; “Electric Blue,” now reaching its 21st-anniversary vinyl reissue, is among his earlier solo releases. Clarke has continued to work outside Erasure as well, contributing to and remixing for other artists’ projects, including Doublespeak, his covers collaboration with Blancmange, announced earlier in 2026. The Erasure Information Service newsletter, edited by Richard Evans, has served as the duo and Bell’s primary direct fan-communication channel for reissue updates, solo activity and, as of this newsletter, hints toward a new Erasure album project still to be formally announced.

items.body: Cocteau Twins released their fifth studio album, “Blue Bell Knoll,” through 4AD on 19 September 1988. Capitol Records licensed the record from 4AD for North America, making it the first Cocteau Twins album to receive major-label distribution in the United States. The dream pop album turns 38 this year. Vocalist Elizabeth Fraser named the album after Bluebell Knoll, a peak in southern Utah. Guitarist Robin Guthrie produced the record and handled keyboards along with synth and drum machine programming, while Simon Raymonde played bass and keyboards. All ten tracks are credited to Fraser, Guthrie and Raymonde: the title track, “Athol-Brose,” “Carolyn’s Fingers,” “For Phoebe Still a Baby,” “The Itchy Glowbo Blow,” “Cico Buff,” “Suckling the Mender,” “Spooning Good Singing Gum,” “A Kissed Out Red Floatboat” and “Ella Megalast Burls Forever.” Fraser sang the whole album in her own constructed language. Raymonde later described the sessions as a settled period for the trio: “it really felt like a period of creativity and freedom, we were all getting on great musically and socially, Liz and Robin were about to have a baby, I was about to get married, there was lots of joy around. Very productive! It was a really fun record to make.” Fraser connected that ease to the decision to drop conventional lyrics, telling The Quietus in 2017: “I gained so much from [inventing language] […] Writing Blue Bell Knoll I had a wonderful freedom to put lyrics aside and not to worry [about people’s opinions].” The album reached number 15 on the UK Albums Chart and number 109 on the US Billboard 200, and “Carolyn’s Fingers” climbed to number two on the US Alternative Airplay chart. Promotional videos accompanied “Carolyn’s Fingers” and “Cico Buff.” The vinyl edition came in a limited gatefold sleeve, and the album was the first 4AD title issued commercially on DAT. After 4AD reclaimed the North American rights to its back catalogue, Guthrie remastered “Blue Bell Knoll” for a 2003 reissue, and the album was repressed on 180g vinyl in 2014. It streams on Spotify. About Cocteau Twins Cocteau Twins formed in 1979 in Grangemouth, Scotland, around guitarist Robin Guthrie and bassist Will Heggie, who took the band name from a song by fellow Scots Simple Minds. Guthrie met Elizabeth Fraser in Falkirk in 1981 and asked her to sing. The group signed to 4AD and issued its debut album, “Garlands,” in 1982, followed by “Head over Heels” in 1983. Heggie left that year and Simon Raymonde replaced him, arriving in time for 1984’s “Treasure.” Two albums came in 1986: “Victorialand,” recorded largely as a duo while Raymonde worked on This Mortal Coil, and “The Moon and the Melodies,” a collaboration with ambient composer Harold Budd. “Blue Bell Knoll” followed on 19 September 1988 and became the band’s first record to enter the US Billboard 200, a direct result of the Capitol licensing deal. “Heaven or Las Vegas” arrived in 1990 and closed the group’s run on 4AD; Cocteau Twins then signed to Fontana for “Four-Calendar Café” (1993) and “Milk & Kisses” (1996), and disbanded in 1997. All three have kept working since. Side-Line covered Raymonde’s Bella Union label presenting the debut album by his project Lost Horizons in 2017, Guthrie’s ‘Riviera’ EP in 2021 and his ‘Springtime’ EP in 2022, and reported that Fraser had returned with her first new material in 13 years in 2022. “Blue Bell Knoll” turns 38 this year, the record that opened the American market to the band two years before its 4AD run ended.
